title: METALICA:METAdynamics and repLICA exchange for enhanced diffusion sampling

paper.title: METALICA: METAdynamics and repLICA exchange for enhanced diffusion sampling
paper.abstract: Abstract Many proteins function through transitions between conformational states, yet rare states are rarely sampled by diffusion models trained on an equilibrium ensemble, demanding better sampling methods. We introduce METALICA, which implements Metadynamics on a pretrained diffusion model via Replica Exchange. It accumulates a bias potential along a Collective Variable, repels new samples from previous ones through biased sampling, and reweights samples onto the unbiased distribution. METALICA holds one replica per diffusion level, forming a Markov Chain that evolves through inter-replica communication and is refined in place as the bias grows. METALICA is the dual of sequential control, in which Sequential Monte Carlo parallelizes the sampler over a batch of particles. Parallelism over the levels of the diffusion-time schedule instead allows METALICA to generate samples from long chains, essential for the discovery of rare events, with accuracy set by run length rather than by the memory available. We validate on a bimodal target with known free energies, then apply METALICA to the unfolding of a protein. At a budget for which sequential control yields no unfolded structure, METALICA populates the basin and resolves a second free energy minimum.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Proteins undergo functionally important transitions between distinct conformational states ( Henzler-Wildman and Kern, 2007 ; Boehr et al., 2009 ) , and are thus better represented by conformational ensembles and energy landscapes than by a single static structure ( Onuchic et al., 1997 ) . Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations are widely used to generate such ensembles ( Hollingsworth and Dror, 2018 ) , but often struggle to explore complex energy landscapes ( Hénin et al., 2022 ) . Enhanced sampling techniques such as Umbrella Sampling ( Torrie and Valleau, 1977 ) and Metadynamics ( Laio and Parrinello, 2002 ) address this by biasing along predefined Collective Variables (CVs), encouraging sampling of under-populated regions ( Hénin et al., 2022 ) . However, such simulations remain computationally demanding, and since samples derive from time-evolving trajectories, they are inherently correlated. In parallel, diffusion models, often trained or fine-tuned on MD data to learn conformational distributions, have shown strong success generating uncorrelated biomolecular ensembles, including ensembles for proteins ( Lewis et al., 2025 ) . Unlike MD, they need not overcome free-energy barriers, but since they sample from the learned equilibrium distribution, rare, yet functionally important, conformations remain hard to capture without prohibitively large sample sizes ( Noé et al., 2019 ) . Inspired by the enhanced sampling approaches for MD simulations, recent works have tried to solve the rare event sampling problem by integrating Umbrella Sampling ( Richman et al., 2026 ) and Metadynamics ( Xie et al., 2026 ; Lam et al., 2026 ) into diffusion models. Rather than sample the learned data distribution p 0 ​ ( x ) p_{0}(x) , these methods tilt the target to p 0 ​ ( x ) ​ exp ⁡ ( r 0 ​ ( x ) ) p_{0}(x)\exp(r_{0}(x)) , with r 0 r_{0} being a reward function intended to boost the probability of rare states. Sampling from the tilted targets is achieved via Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC)-based methods such as the Twisted Diffusion Sampler (TDS, Wu et al. (2023) ) or the Feynman-Kac Corrector (FKC, Skreta et al. (2025) ), where a fresh batch of samples is initialized with pure noise and steered towards each of the target tilted distributions. After gathering batches of samples, each under a different bias potential, they are pooled using the Multistate Bennett Acceptance Ratio (MBAR) ( Shirts and Chodera, 2008 ) or Weighted Histogram Analysis Method (WHAM) ( Kumar et al., 1992 ) to reconstruct the unbiased distribution p 0 p_{0} . The accuracy of enhanced diffusion sampling depends on SMC-based approaches correctly sampling tilted target distributions, which requires large batch sizes and small denoising steps ( Phillips et al., 2024 ; Ren et al., 2026 ) . Otherwise, lineage collapse and reduced Effective Sample Size (ESS) degrade performance. This worsens for rare events requiring stronger tilts ( Xie et al., 2026 ) , since only a tiny fraction of samples fall in the rare region, making current implementations inefficient and inaccurate under realistic memory and compute constraints. In response, we introduce METALICA, an enhanced sampling method integrating METAdynamics into diffusion models via repLICA exchange. Rather than batch sampling, METALICA runs a single Markov Chain with replicas at different denoising steps in parallel, sampling sequentially.

Because an RE chain is just a state, its target can be changed mid-run, and the current state remains a well-equilibrated start for the new target when the change is small. METALICA therefore refines the target in place: the chain carries over from iteration k k to k + 1 k+1 with no fresh burn-in, which sequential control cannot do since it restarts from noise at every k k .

sections.heading: A computational duality.
sections.text: MetaDiff and METALICA accept any bias-update rule and share ( 2 ); they differ only in which axis the sampler parallelizes over, and that decides what one pays for more samples. Under sequential control, more samples means more particles: memory grows with N N , wall-clock does not, and the samples are nearly independent, but every particle is annealed from noise again at each bias update, so accuracy at each iteration is whatever a batch of size N N can deliver. Under parallel control, more samples means more steps of the same chain: wall-clock grows with N N , memory does not, and each step starts from an equilibrated state and pays no restart at a bias update ( 10 ), so accuracy is set by chain length rather than by memory. The two spend the same N ​ M NM score evaluations per iteration and neither dominates: MetaDiff is the right tool when memory is plentiful and time is short, METALICA when memory is the binding constraint, which is the case for rare events, where a batch must be large enough to represent the rare region before any bias can be deposited from it. Appendix F.3 measures this trade-off (Figures 3 and 4 ).

sections.text: We first test METALICA in a toy setting where p 0 p_{0} is known: a bimodal Gaussian mixture on ℝ \mathbb{R} with modes centered at μ = ± 3 \mu=\pm 3 of equal width ( σ mix = 0.5 \sigma_{\mathrm{mix}}=0.5 ). sections.heading: Proteins.
sections.text: We further apply our enhanced sampling to BioEmu ( Lewis et al., 2025 ) , a real-world diffusion model trained on a large collection of protein structures and fine-tuned on MD trajectories, capable of rapidly generating approximate conformational ensembles. However, for rare events such as protein unfolding, it still requires a dramatic number of samples to observe even a single unfolded conformation. Therefore, we leverage Fraction of Native Contacts (FNC) as our CV ξ \xi , whose values ξ ⁡ ( x ) \xi(x) lie in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , to separate the folded state Ω A = { ξ > 0.5 } \Omega_{\mathrm{A}}=\{\xi>0.5\} from the unfolded state Ω B = { ξ < 0.5 } \Omega_{\mathrm{B}}=\{\xi<0.5\} . We take 1BTA from the Protein Data Bank (PDB, Berman et al. (2000) ), among the most stable proteins in ProThermDB ( Nikam et al., 2021 ) . A separate pool of 20,000 20{,}000 unbiased BioEmu draws for this protein contains a single unfolded structure. On the other hand, drawing 6,000 6{,}000 samples using METALICA ( N = 150 N=150 ) not only generates many unfolded structures, but also reveals a double-basin free energy landscape and estimates Δ ​ F ^ ξ = 13.3 \Delta\hat{F}^{\xi}=13.3 with ≈ 680 {\approx}680 rare samples generated (Figure 2 ). More details about this experiment are in Appendix F.4 .

sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: In this work, we showed how the Replica Exchange paradigm can diversely sample from a broad Collective Variable range through communications between replicas of a Markov chain ladder. Replacing batch parallelism with replica parallelism decouples accuracy from batch size: METALICA’s long sequential runs make free energy estimation affordable under memory constraints, and online refinement lets one chain follow the bias potential as it grows. METALICA does inherit the limitations of Metadynamics: it needs Collective Variables that separate the states of interest, and its samples are consecutive states of one chain rather than independent draws. Separately, what it estimates is the free energy landscape of the model that generated the samples, not of the underlying physical system.

sections.heading: Block deposition.
sections.text: Both methods emit N N samples per iteration and lay them down one hill at a time, each hill tempered against the bias in force when it is laid rather than against the frozen V k V_{k} . METALICA’s samples x k ( n ) x^{(n)}_{k} are unweighted states of one chain, so the iteration’s height budget h h is split evenly across them: starting from b k ≡ 0 b_{k}\equiv 0 and applying, in order for n = 1 , … , N n=1,\dots,N , b k ​ ( ω ) ← b k ​ ( ω ) + h N ​ exp ⁡ ( − V k ​ ( ξ ⁡ ( x k ( n ) ) ) + b k ​ ( ξ ⁡ ( x k ( n ) ) ) γ − 1 ) ​ exp ⁡ ( − ∥ ω − ξ ⁡ ( x k ( n ) ) ∥ 2 2 ​ σ hill 2 ) , b_{k}(\omega)\;\leftarrow\;b_{k}(\omega)+\frac{h}{N}\exp\!\left(-\frac{V_{k}(\xi(x^{(n)}_{k}))+b_{k}(\xi(x^{(n)}_{k}))}{\gamma-1}\right)\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert\omega-\xi(x^{(n)}_{k})\rVert^{2}}{2\sigma_{\mathrm{hill}}^{2}}\right), (13) so each hill is damped by V k + b k V_{k}+b_{k} , the bias already accumulated within the block, and the iteration closes with V k + 1 = V k + b k V_{k+1}=V_{k}+b_{k} . sections.heading: Schedule and boundary levels.
sections.text: The M + 1 M+1 times of the schedule are the discretization grid of the reverse process itself, uniformly spaced on [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , so a level-to-level move is one step of the integrator. Following Syed et al. [2022] , step n n proposes exchanges on all pairs ( m − 1 , m ) (m-1,m) with m ≡ n ( mod 2 ) m\equiv n\pmod{2} ; the proposals within a step are independent and run in parallel. No local exploration move is applied at intermediate levels in our experiments. The bottom particle X n 0 X^{0}_{n} is recorded at every step as a sample from π 0 \pi_{0} .

METALICA: METAdynamics and repLICA exchange for enhanced diffusion sampling Alireza Omidi * Affiliation: University of British Columbia Email: aomidi@student.ubc.ca Jiajun He Affiliation: University of Cambridge Email: jh2383@cam.ac.uk Jörg Gsponer † Affiliation: University of British Columbia Email: gsponer@msl.ubc.ca Saifuddin Syed † Affiliation: University of British Columbia Email: saif.syed@stat.ubc.ca Abstract Many proteins function through transitions between conformational states, yet rare states are rarely sampled by diffusion models trained on an equilibrium ensemble, demanding better sampling methods. We introduce METALICA, which implements Metadynamics on a pretrained diffusion model via Replica Exchange. It accumulates a bias potential along a Collective Variable, repels new samples from previous ones through biased sampling, and reweights samples onto the unbiased distribution. METALICA holds one replica per diffusion level, forming a Markov Chain that evolves through inter-replica communication and is refined in place as the bias grows. METALICA is the dual of sequential control, in which Sequential Monte Carlo parallelizes the sampler over a batch of particles. Parallelism over the levels of the diffusion-time schedule instead allows METALICA to generate samples from long chains, essential for the discovery of rare events, with accuracy set by run length rather than by the memory available. We validate on a bimodal target with known free energies, then apply METALICA to the unfolding of a protein. At a budget for which sequential control yields no unfolded structure, METALICA populates the basin and resolves a second free energy minimum. 1 Introduction Proteins undergo functionally important transitions between distinct conformational states ( Henzler-Wildman and Kern, 2007 ; Boehr et al., 2009 ) , and are thus better represented by conformational ensembles and energy landscapes than by a single static structure ( Onuchic et al., 1997 ) . Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations are widely used to generate such ensembles ( Hollingsworth and Dror, 2018 ) , but often struggle to explore complex energy landscapes ( Hénin et al., 2022 ) . Enhanced sampling techniques such as Umbrella Sampling ( Torrie and Valleau, 1977 ) and Metadynamics ( Laio and Parrinello, 2002 ) address this by biasing along predefined Collective Variables (CVs), encouraging sampling of under-populated regions ( Hénin et al., 2022 ) . However, such simulations remain computationally demanding, and since samples derive from time-evolving trajectories, they are inherently correlated. In parallel, diffusion models, often trained or fine-tuned on MD data to learn conformational distributions, have shown strong success generating uncorrelated biomolecular ensembles, including ensembles for proteins ( Lewis et al., 2025 ) . Unlike MD, they need not overcome free-energy barriers, but since they sample from the learned equilibrium distribution, rare, yet functionally important, conformations remain hard to capture without prohibitively large sample sizes ( Noé et al., 2019 ) . Inspired by the enhanced sampling approaches for MD simulations, recent works have tried to solve the rare event sampling problem by integrating Umbrella Sampling ( Richman et al., 2026 ) and Metadynamics ( Xie et al., 2026 ; Lam et al., 2026 ) into diffusion models. Rather than sample the learned data distribution p 0 ​ ( x ) p_{0}(x) , these methods tilt the target to p 0 ​ ( x ) ​ exp ⁡ ( r 0 ​ ( x ) ) p_{0}(x)\exp(r_{0}(x)) , with r 0 r_{0} being a reward function intended to boost the probability of rare states. Sampling from the tilted targets is achieved via Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC)-based methods such as the Twisted Diffusion Sampler (TDS, Wu et al. (2023) ) or the Feynman-Kac Corrector (FKC, Skreta et al. (2025) ), where a fresh batch of samples is initialized with pure noise and steered towards each of the target tilted distributions. After gathering batches of samples, each under a different bias potential, they are pooled using the Multistate Bennett Acceptance Ratio (MBAR) ( Shirts and Chodera, 2008 ) or Weighted Histogram Analysis Method (WHAM) ( Kumar et al., 1992 ) to reconstruct the unbiased distribution p 0 p_{0} . The accuracy of enhanced diffusion sampling depends on SMC-based approaches correctly sampling tilted target distributions, which requires large batch sizes and small denoising steps ( Phillips et al., 2024 ; Ren et al., 2026 ) . Otherwise, lineage collapse and reduced Effective Sample Size (ESS) degrade performance. This worsens for rare events requiring stronger tilts ( Xie et al., 2026 ) , since only a tiny fraction of samples fall in the rare region, making current implementations inefficient and inaccurate under realistic memory and compute constraints. In response, we introduce METALICA, an enhanced sampling method integrating METAdynamics into diffusion models via repLICA exchange. A computational duality. MetaDiff and METALICA accept any bias-update rule and share ( 2 ); they differ only in which axis the sampler parallelizes over, and that decides what one pays for more samples. Under sequential control, more samples means more particles: memory grows with N N , wall-clock does not, and the samples are nearly independent, but every particle is annealed from noise again at each bias update, so accuracy at each iteration is whatever a batch of size N N can deliver. Under parallel control, more samples means more steps of the same chain: wall-clock grows with N N , memory does not, and each step starts from an equilibrated state and pays no restart at a bias update ( 10 ), so accuracy is set by chain length rather than by memory. The two spend the same N ​ M NM score evaluations per iteration and neither dominates: MetaDiff is the right tool when memory is plentiful and time is short, METALICA when memory is the binding constraint, which is the case for rare events, where a batch must be large enough to represent the rare region before any bias can be deposited from it. More details about this experiment are in Appendix F.4 . 5 Discussion In this work, we showed how the Replica Exchange paradigm can diversely sample from a broad Collective Variable range through communications between replicas of a Markov chain ladder. Replacing batch parallelism with replica parallelism decouples accuracy from batch size: METALICA’s long sequential runs make free energy estimation affordable under memory constraints, and online refinement lets one chain follow the bias potential as it grows. METALICA does inherit the limitations of Metadynamics: it needs Collective Variables that separate the states of interest, and its samples are consecutive states of one chain rather than independent draws. Separately, what it estimates is the free energy landscape of the model that generated the samples, not of the underlying physical system.
